title: The Gentleman's Guide to Air Travel
author: Ways of a Gentleman
summary: This article argues that the degradation of air travel manners is not inevitable but a choice — and that a gentleman's response is to bring style and civility back to the experience through how he dresses, how he treats fellow passengers, and how he conducts himself under stress. The author connects dressing well while flying to self-respect and courtesy toward others, arguing that comfort does not require looking disheveled and that specific clothing choices (oxford shirt, stretch chinos, unstructured blazer) achieve both. The piece moves through practical domains: armrest etiquette (middle seat gets both), noise discipline, overhead bin protocol, how to treat flight attendants (with genuine courtesy rather than performative niceness), managing gate and boarding situations with patience, and the specific challenges of red-eye flights. The article's deeper argument is that how a man carries himself in logistically stressed, public, shared-space situations is a test of character — the gentleman's behavior in an airport is the same character he brings to every room, revealing who he actually is.
points: Dressing well on a plane is not about discomfort but about the false equation of comfort with looking disheveled — specific travel-friendly clothing choices (stretch chinos, unstructured blazer, loafers) achieve both without compromise.

Armrest etiquette has a clear rule: the middle seat deserves both armrests, full stop — window and aisle passengers should not suggest otherwise, and a gentleman respects this without having to be asked.

How a man treats flight attendants reveals his character: genuine courtesy (not performative niceness or demanding entitlement) toward people in service roles is among the most reliable signals of who a person actually is.

Public, logistically stressed shared-space environments — airports, boarding queues, cramped cabins — are tests of character precisely because the social pressure to behave poorly is highest and the social enforcement is weakest.

The gentleman's code is environment-invariant: the same calm, courteous, self-possessed man who dresses well and gives up the armrest on a flight is the man who shows up that way everywhere — style and civility are not performances but expressions of character.
quotes: There was a time when air travel was exceptional. It was a special occasion marked by fine clothing and dignified behavior. Passengers dressed in suits and ties, and treated the journey as an experience, not just a means of travel. While those golden days of flight might be long gone, some of the ideals are just as relevant now as ever.

Dressing well while traveling is still a demonstration of one's self-respect and courtesy toward others. Likewise, gentlemanly behavior while flying is a testament to your character in what has become an often stressful environment.

Some will argue that dressing well while flying is uncomfortable and perhaps even impossible. I wholeheartedly disagree with that notion. Yes, a tailored suit may not match the comfort of sweatpants, but we should not confuse comfort with laziness. One can absolutely dress comfortably without looking disheveled.
Armrest etiquette: The middle seat deserves both armrests. Window and aisle passengers should not suggest otherwise.

Getting along with a principal doesn't mean you have to flatter incessantly or be a total doormat — and the same principle holds on a plane. A gentleman is not a pushover, but he is also not a problem.
Through dressing well, manners, and respect for others, we can set the example for others in the air.
